topics.topic: Anchor for resolving relative configuration paths on later rereads
questions: Is a relative configuration path resolved from the process working directory captured at startup, or from whatever the working directory is on each later token-list reread?
What directory anchors a relative configuration-file path for every later re-read?

For later configuration re-reads, is a relative path resolved from the working directory captured at startup or from the process working directory at each read, and is the kernel forbidden to change that directory?

quotes:
Before evaluating each request the kernel reads the configuration file and
   compares the SHA-256 of its bytes with that of the last read; when they differ,
   or the file cannot be read, it re-reads it (K-15) and takes from it only the
   token list.

Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests (A20 rule 3) — the path as
   given, an absolute one walked from the root directory and a relative one
   from the working directory;
judgement.divergence: One implementation resolves the relative path once against the startup working directory; another resolves it against the process working directory on every reread, so after a directory change the owner and agent callers may be authenticated from different configuration files.
judgement.why: The reread rule does not fix whether the relative path's working-directory anchor is captured once or reevaluated.

topics.topic: Crash-safe ordering and durability semantics for file publication and database commit
questions: What does “flushed” mean, where is the temporary file created, what directories are synchronized, and in what order do file publication and the SQLite commit occur so that a crash or power loss cannot leave a durable record naming a missing or incomplete file?
What publication and flush sequence guarantees that no committed record names a missing or incomplete file after a crash?
What exact ordering between temporary-file creation, flush, rename, directory flush and database commit prevents a committed record from naming a missing or incomplete file after a crash?
Does ‘crash’ include host or power loss, and what exact durability operation constitutes ‘flushed’ for the file, containing directory and SQLite transaction?

judgement.why: This is the same crash-durable file-publication and database-commit ordering question already judged in P4, and its cited State 2 passage is unchanged.

precedent.topic: Filesystem and SQLite flush, publication, commit, and recovery protocol for crash durability
quotes:
Value bytes and spooled files are written to a temporary file, flushed, checked
   against their digest and size, and then renamed into place; a completed file a record names is
   never overwritten — a spooled file no record names, left by a change that
   failed, is replaced at its position.
precedent.why: The topic concerns unchanged A18 publication and durability language, which the reopening change did not affect.

topics.topic: Exact privacy, ownership, type, and permission requirements for store objects
questions: What exact ownership, mode, file-type and traversal checks make the data directory and everything in it “private,” and are those properties checked again when entries are opened or created after startup?
What exact ownership, permissions, ACL, link-count and file-type conditions must every data-directory object satisfy at start?
What exact owner, file type and permission checks make the directory, database, auxiliary SQLite files, value area, fixtures and spool ‘private’, and are those checks repeated after startup?

judgement.why: This is the same exact private ownership and permission question already judged in P2, and the relevant store rule is unchanged.

precedent.topic: Exact private ownership and permission requirements and when they are rechecked
quotes: The directory and everything in it are private to the kernel's user; the kernel refuses to start otherwise.
precedent.why: The topic concerns A18's unchanged data-directory privacy rule, and the Linux/O_NOFOLLOW change to A17 and A20 did not make that existing question matter.

topics.topic: Exclusive data-directory lock primitive, lifecycle, and stale artifacts
questions: What Linux locking primitive and lock object define exclusivity, when is the lock acquired and released, and how are stale lock artifacts after a crash treated?
What exact lock constitutes ownership of a data directory, and how is it safely created, acquired and retained?
What object and Linux locking operation define this lock, when is it acquired and released, and how are stale lock artifacts distinguished from a live holder?

judgement.why: This is the same exclusive-lock object, primitive, acquisition and lifetime question already judged in P3.

precedent.topic: Exclusive store lock object, primitive, acquisition, lifetime, and descriptor inheritance
quotes:
At start it takes an exclusive lock in the data
   directory; a second process on the same directory refuses to start.
precedent.why: The lock requirement is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect its object, primitive or lifetime.

topics.topic: Initialization or rejection of missing, partial, or damaged store layouts
questions: If the data directory, database, content areas, spool area, or lock object does not yet exist, which objects does the kernel create and which missing objects make startup fail?
Which absent or damaged store conditions are initialized, refused, ignored or repaired at startup?
Must the data directory and its required children already exist, may the kernel create any of them, and what happens when only part of the layout exists?

judgement.why: This is the same bootstrap and initialization question for missing store paths and objects already judged in P17.

precedent.topic: Bootstrap behavior for missing data-store paths and objects
quotes:
`refused` naming a data directory that does not exist, the lock held, a
directory not private, or a symbolic link; the start stops. The kernel never
creates the data directory itself: the owner creates it, private to the
kernel's user; inside it `open_store` creates the database schema, the
content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller, the same exception with its own reason; before it propagates MUST write the failing step's name — load_installation, check_installed_instances, open_store, probe_sandbox, recover_in_flight_attempts or recover_running_runs — as one line to standard error, so the step is named there and the reason stays the exception's own; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
precedent.why: State 7 specifies which paths must preexist, which store objects are created, the internal open-store order, and propagation of database or other startup failures.

topics.topic: Safe resolution and validation of the data-directory path and entry types
questions: Does the no-symlink rule cover the configured data-directory path itself and every path component, or only final entries inside an already opened data directory, and what opening procedure prevents check-to-open races?
How is the configured data-directory path resolved and checked?

Does this cover the data-directory path and every ancestor and subdirectory, and what happens when an expected entry is a FIFO, socket, device, mount point or other non-regular type rather than a symbolic link?

judgement.why: This is the same data-directory path resolution and symbolic-link policy question already judged in P21.

precedent.topic: Resolution and symbolic-link policy for the data-directory path
quotes:
Every
   file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link
   found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call
   fail with nothing written.
precedent.why: A18's store traversal requirement is unchanged; making A17's separate configuration traversal more explicit did not alter the store rule.

topics.topic: Startup cleanup targets and handling of inspection or removal failures
questions: Does failure to remove a temporary file or unreferenced value byte stop startup, get ignored like an unremovable ended-run spool directory, or leave the affected object quarantined?
What exact names count as kernel temporary files, and does failure to remove a temporary or unreferenced value stop startup?
Unlike spool-directory removal, what happens if a temporary file or unreferenced value cannot be inspected or removed during startup cleanup?

judgement.why: This is the same startup cleanup-failure behavior question already judged in P16.

precedent.topic: Behavior when startup cleanup of temporary or unreferenced files fails
quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

open_store: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns StoreOpened with data_directory and temporary_files_removed, the count of temporary files removed, unnamed value files not counted; no record, named value file or spool is removed by this call; the spools of ended runs are removed later in the start sequence, by run recovery (A18 rule 4).

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller, the same exception with its own reason; before it propagates MUST write the failing step's name — load_installation, check_installed_instances, open_store, probe_sandbox, recover_in_flight_attempts or recover_running_runs — as one line to standard error, so the step is named there and the reason stays the exception's own; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
precedent.why: State 7 says unnamed fixture values are removed as unnamed value files, active-run spools are not removed by open_store, and any cleanup exception stops startup through the ordered start sequence.

topics.topic: Validation and handling of an existing content-addressed destination
questions: What happens when a file already exists at a content digest but its bytes or recorded size differ from the bytes now being published with that same digest?
How does the store handle an existing digest-named file whose content does not equal the bytes being published?
When the digest-named destination already exists, must its type, size, digest and bytes be verified, and what happens if it is corrupt or different bytes have the same claimed digest?

judgement.why: This is the same handling of an existing mismatched or unreadable digest-named file already judged in P19.

precedent.topic: Handling an existing mismatched or unreadable digest-named file
quotes: put_value_bytes: [PATH_OR_ARTIFACT_POLICY] MUST store the bytes in the content-addressed area under their digest: when a file for that digest already exists it returns without writing; otherwise it writes a temporary file in the same area, flushes and fsyncs it, re-checks its digest and size, and renames it into place without overwriting, so a crash leaves either no file or the complete file and a completed file is never rewritten.

read_value_bytes: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise UnknownReferenceError when the identity names no record, and StoreInternalError when the bytes of an existing record are missing, unreadable, reached through a symbolic link, or differ from the record's digest or size.

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller, the same exception with its own reason; before it propagates MUST write the failing step's name — load_installation, check_installed_instances, open_store, probe_sandbox, recover_in_flight_attempts or recover_running_runs — as one line to standard error, so the step is named there and the reason stays the exception's own; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
precedent.why: State 7 specifies reuse of an existing digest path, validation on reads, the resulting internal error, and startup failure propagation.

topics.topic: Definition and assignment of the global store order
questions: What exactly is a store position and how is the total order assigned across all record types and multi-record transactions?
What is the store order among multiple records created in the same transaction, and does every record type participate in one global order or only records of the same type?

judgement.why: This is the same assignment of store positions across multi-record writes and lifecycle updates already judged in P8.

precedent.topic: Assignment of store positions for multi-record writes and later mutations
quotes: record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] Every record written gets one store position from next_store_position, a single strictly increasing counter shared by all record types, called inside the transaction that writes the record; store order is the order of these positions, every collection the module returns is in store order unless the function says otherwise, and Activation and FlowActivation records are identified by their store_position.

record_change: [DETERMINISM_OR_ORDERING] The records one change writes take their store positions with every StoredValue first, in the order the variant names them, then the other records in the order the field-assignment note of its variant lists them, the elements of a list of records in list order (a RecordRunProgressChange's executions in (node_id, map_index) order); an update keeps the record's position, so positions never depend on record type or database insertion order.

next_store_position: [BEHAVIOR] MUST read the counter row with load_store_position_counter for = models.StoreCounterName store_position, take one more than its last_position, or 1 when no counter row exists yet, write that number back as last_position with upsert_store_position_counter on the same repository, and return it; it is called only by this module inside the transaction of a change, so a change that fails leaves the counter as it was and no two records ever share a position.
precedent.why: State 7 defines allocation, within-change ordering, global monotonicity, and position preservation on lifecycle updates.

topics.topic: Exact startup sequencing and precedence among startup failures
questions: What is the exact startup order, especially whether ended-run spool cleanup uses stored status or the state derived by A14?
In what order are the lock, data-directory validation, symlink scan, cleanup, SQLite opening, sandbox probe and A14 recovery performed, and which failure is reported when several fail?

judgement.why: This is the same ordering and precedence question for startup validation, cleanup and recovery already judged in P5.

precedent.topic: Ordering and precedence of startup validation, recovery, and cleanup
quotes: run_start_sequence: [ORCHESTRATION] MUST call, in exactly this order and each exactly once: load_installation with config_path; check_installed_instances with the loaded Installation; open_store with that Installation's data_directory; probe_sandbox; recover_in_flight_attempts; recover_running_runs (A03 rule 8, A09 rule 1, A14 rule 5, A18).

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, opened as a directory without following links and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
precedent.why: State 7 fixes both the overall startup sequence and the complete first-failure order inside store opening.

topics.topic: Handling potentially blocking non-regular configuration-file components
questions: How is the kernel guaranteed not to block or cause device-specific effects when it must open the final component before checking that it is a regular file, given that Linux does not make `O_NONBLOCK` effective for every file type?
What must happen when opening a non-regular final component can block despite `O_NONBLOCK`?

quotes:
Here and in rule 2 the path is opened component by component without
   following a symbolic link at any of them, each component with Linux's
   `O_NOFOLLOW`, whose presence no code tests (A20 rule 3) — the path as
   given, an absolute one walked from the root directory and a relative one
   from the working directory; each directory on the way opened with
   `O_PATH` and `O_DIRECTORY`, so a directory the kernel's user may only
   search is passed, and the last component for reading with `O_NONBLOCK`
   as well, so a component that is no regular file is refused by the checks
   rather than waited on;

Another system, or
   a Linux or file system on which a call these rules rely on — opening with
   the flags they name, locking, renaming, flushing — does not act as Linux
   documents it, is unsupported: the kernel neither tests for it nor defines
   what it does there;
judgement.divergence: One implementation performs the prescribed open and can block or trigger device-specific behavior before checking the file type; another first applies additional type-safe opening or inspection and immediately refuses, which the owner notices as a hanging or side-effecting start or reread versus a prompt refusal.
judgement.why: The rules require opening before the regular-file check but do not define behavior for Linux non-regular objects whose documented open behavior can still block or have effects despite O_NONBLOCK.

topics.topic: Observable event defining concurrent request arrival order
questions: Which observable event fixes the serialization order of concurrent requests?

What event defines arrival order when requests are received concurrently or only partially received: connection acceptance, first byte, complete MCP message, successful framing, or insertion into a single queue?

judgement.why: This is the same question about the event defining arrival order for concurrent MCP requests already judged in P1.

precedent.topic: Event that defines arrival order for concurrent MCP requests
quotes:
Surface requests are handled one at a time in the order they arrive: one request, including the run
   advancement it causes (A13), ends before the next begins, so an approval, a
   cancellation and a resume of one run never race.
precedent.why: The serialization sentence is unchanged, and the reopening change did not affect concurrent-request ordering.

topics.topic: Required behavior when running on a non-Linux host
questions: Must the kernel explicitly refuse to start on a non-Linux host, or may it attempt to run with wholly undefined behavior?
Must the kernel positively identify Linux and refuse startup elsewhere, or does it perform no host check and merely provide no defined behavior on another system?

quotes:
A release runs on Linux and
   on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18). Another system, or
   a Linux or file system on which a call these rules rely on — opening with
   the flags they name, locking, renaming, flushing — does not act as Linux
   documents it, is unsupported: the kernel neither tests for it nor defines
   what it does there;
judgement.why: The text explicitly says another host is unsupported and that the kernel neither tests for it nor defines its behavior there.

topics.topic: Supported Linux syscall, kernel, and filesystem compatibility baseline
questions: Which Linux documentation and syscall semantics define the supported baseline when kernel versions and file-system implementations differ, particularly for `O_PATH`, `O_NOFOLLOW`, locking, rename and persistence after flushing?
Against which Linux semantics must opening, locking, renaming and flushing be implemented and tested when different kernel and filesystem versions provide different guarantees?

quotes:
A release runs on Linux and
   on no other host, no version named (owner, 2026-10-18). Another system, or
   a Linux or file system on which a call these rules rely on — opening with
   the flags they name, locking, renaming, flushing — does not act as Linux
   documents it, is unsupported: the kernel neither tests for it nor defines
   what it does there;
judgement.divergence: One implementer supports the semantics and feature set of the release builder's current kernel and filesystem; another targets an older or narrower Linux ABI, so the owner sees the same installation start and operate on one Linux system but fail or behave as unsupported on another.
judgement.why: No Linux version, documentation baseline, minimum syscall feature set or filesystem durability contract identifies which differing documented semantics define support.

topics.topic: Symlink-safe opening and validation of SQLite auxiliary files
questions: How must SQLite-created auxiliary files be opened and checked so that a symlink inserted after startup cannot be followed?
How is this guarantee enforced for the SQLite database and SQLite-created journal, WAL and shared-memory files, whose opens may be performed internally by SQLite?

quotes:
Every
   file of the directory is opened without following symbolic links; a link
   found at start stops the start, and one found later makes that store call
   fail with nothing written.
judgement.why: The topic concerns A18's unchanged store symlink rule, and the reopening changes to configuration-file traversal and the Linux support boundary did not alter SQLite auxiliary-file handling.

topics.topic: Atomic transaction boundaries for multi-record actions
questions: Which records and state transitions of a multi-record action must be one change and therefore atomic, where another decision does not explicitly name the store calls?

topics.topic: Irrevocable success boundary and post-commit failure handling for store calls
questions: At what point is a store call irrevocably successful, and what happens if cleanup, acknowledgement or another operation fails after commit?
